Watts and kWh: power is different from energy

Understand the difference between the number on an appliance label and the number on your electricity meter.

Vijeron · Updated 9 October 2026

Watts describe a rate

Watts (W) tell you how quickly a device uses energy at a moment in time. A 100 W rating does not mean the device always uses 100 kWh. To compare devices, you also need operating time and an idea of whether the power draw stays constant. A rating plate is often a nominal value, not a measurement over a whole day.

kWh add up energy

A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of energy. A steady 1,000 W load running for one hour uses 1 kWh. A 100 W load running for ten hours also uses 1 kWh. A small load left on continuously can therefore use more energy than a powerful device used briefly.

Keep the units straight

Convert watts to kilowatts by dividing by 1,000, then multiply by hours. If a label already states annual kWh, do not multiply it by hours again: it already reports energy for the stated period. Read the test period and conditions on the label.

A worked example

Example: a 10 W lamp used for 5 hours consumes 10 × 5 ÷ 1,000 = 0.05 kWh. This is arithmetic, not a product measurement.

Avoid this mistake

Common error: saying a 100 W device consumes 100 kWh without specifying operating time.
